rationale: The sources give the difference-quotient definition of differentiability. The item adapts it to arbitrary intervals, relative-domain endpoint limits, isolated-point exclusion, and an explicit uniqueness clause.

The notes state Carathéodory’s characterization with the same continuous-factor equivalence and value at the base point. The item adds global uniqueness of the factor and arbitrary relative-domain bookkeeping, so it is a semantic adaptation; the proof is likewise locally expanded.
Both sources state that differentiability implies continuity. The proof is a local Carathéodory-factor argument rather than a verbatim source proof.

The source gives the equivalent first-order linear approximation with an error term tending to zero. The item adds the uniqueness/existence packaging for the affine slope and relative-domain conventions, so both statement and proof are semantic adaptations.
The source states the sum, scalar, product, and quotient rules under the same differentiability and nonzero-denominator hypotheses. The item consolidates them and supplies a Carathéodory-style proof.

The source states the power and polynomial differentiation rules. The item packages the zero exponent separately, adds negative integral powers on the punctured line, and spells out canonical-natural finite-sum indexing, so it is a semantic adaptation proved internally by induction.
The sources state the real chain rule with the same derivative product. The proof is an adapted continuous-factor argument that handles relative domains.

The sources give the inverse-function derivative formula for a continuous strictly monotone function with nonzero derivative. The item packages that theorem with the converse zero-derivative obstruction and explicit interval-image limit-point conditions.
The source gives the standard local maximum and minimum definitions on a real domain. The item’s relative-neighbourhood wording is equivalent.
The sources state Fermat’s theorem that a derivative at an interior local extremum is zero. The proof expands the one-sided sign comparison in the repository’s relative-domain notation.
The sources state Rolle’s theorem with continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on its interior. The proof explicitly treats the constant and interior-extremum cases.
The source states Cauchy’s mean value theorem in the cross-multiplied form used by the item. The proof constructs the usual auxiliary function and applies Rolle’s theorem.
The sources state the mean value theorem with exactly the closed-interval continuity and open-interval differentiability hypotheses. The proof specializes Cauchy’s theorem to the identity function.
The source gives the standard zero-derivative-implies-constant corollary of the mean value theorem. The item supplies the interval endpoint bookkeeping.

The sources give the derivative-sign tests for monotonicity and the converse sign necessity. The item combines weak and strict conclusions, relative endpoints, and the differentiable-interior converse in one theorem.
The source derives the Lipschitz estimate from a uniform derivative bound using the mean value theorem. The item adds the explicit uniform-continuity consequence.
The mathematical conventions summarize standard derivative, endpoint, and algebra facts from the sources, but the item also contains repository-specific sequencing and dependency commentary.
The source states endpoint continuity as an essential mean-value-theorem hypothesis. The item formulates the negation as a false statement and develops an explicit endpoint-discontinuous witness.

Hunter gives the exact x-cubed example: it is strictly increasing while its derivative vanishes at zero. The McGill notes support the derivative framework and cubic derivative only, not the strict-increase attribution. The item packages Hunter's standard counterexample against the stated false implication.
The source supplies the power and algebra rules underlying polynomial differentiation. The particular displayed polynomial computations and their stepwise derivation are worked specializations.
The source gives the absolute-value function as the standard continuous function not differentiable at zero, with conflicting one-sided difference quotients. The proof expands that computation.

Hunter gives x cubed as strictly increasing while its derivative vanishes at zero and records the inverse consequence. The McGill notes support the derivative framework and cubic derivative only, not the strict-increase attribution. The item verifies the properties using the library's power, monotonicity, and inverse results.
The source gives the chain rule and power-rule examples. The item’s chosen composite-polynomial calculation and fully cited factorization are a local worked specialization.
The sources derive inverse-function differentiation and power derivatives. The item specializes these to the positive nth-root map and records the endpoint limitation explicitly.
The source identifies endpoint continuity as part of the mean value theorem. The item supplies a simple endpoint-modified affine witness and computes why no mean-value point exists.
The source restricts Fermat’s theorem to interior extrema. The item gives the canonical identity-function endpoint counterexample and checks the nonzero derivative.
The source gives derivative-bound consequences of the mean value theorem. The square-root increment estimate is a locally chosen specialization using the inverse-rule derivative.

Hunter supports the bounded-derivative implication. MIT's notes explicitly give the square-root function on $[0,1]$ as non-Lipschitz via an unbounded difference-quotient sequence. The item punctures the endpoint to $(0,1]$ and proves both the unbounded derivative and the punctured-domain Lipschitz contradiction locally.
The source states Cauchy’s theorem safely in cross-multiplied form. The item constructs a polynomial example where the denominator derivative vanishes, so the informal quotient form is undefined.
The sources define partitions, subintervals, mesh, and refinement. The item consolidates these with indexing, common-refinement, and finite-list conventions.
The sources define lower and upper Darboux sums using subinterval infima and suprema. The item adds oscillation identities and explicit boundedness conventions.
The sources state that refinement increases lower sums and decreases upper sums. The proof reduces to one-point insertion and then iterates over finitely many new points.
The sources define lower and upper Darboux integrals as the supremum and infimum of the corresponding sums and define integrability by equality.

The sources give the elementary Darboux bounds between the global infimum and supremum times interval length. The proof is an expanded finite-sum derivation; the item’s separate equality-characterization remark is not supported and is flagged for repair.

The sources state the Darboux criterion: integrability is equivalent to arbitrarily small upper-minus-lower sums. The proof expands both directions using refinement and supremum/infimum approximation.
The source defines tagged partitions, Riemann sums, and convergence over sufficiently fine partitions. The item integrates these with the repository’s mesh and Darboux notation.
The source proves equivalence of Darboux and tagged-partition Riemann integrability for bounded functions. The item supplies a fully explicit two-direction construction, including finite tag choices.
The sources prove that every continuous function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable. The item uses uniform continuity to build a small-mesh Darboux partition.
The sources prove that bounded monotone functions on closed intervals are Riemann integrable. The item writes the telescoping uniform-partition estimate for both monotonicity directions.

The university notes state that a bounded function with finitely many discontinuities is Riemann integrable. The item supplies a Darboux proof separating small exceptional intervals from uniformly continuous pieces.

The sources state Lebesgue’s criterion: a bounded function is Riemann integrable exactly when its discontinuity set has measure zero. The item gives a detailed oscillation-superlevel proof in the library’s null/content-zero framework.
The source records the countable-discontinuity consequence of Lebesgue’s criterion. The proof specializes the criterion using countable sets being null.
This is repository-specific dependency and choice-strength accounting across named library results. No located literature source determines this exact internal ledger.
The sources use the bounded Dirichlet indicator to show boundedness alone does not imply Riemann integrability. The item formulates and refutes that standard false statement via Darboux sums.
The sources combine Lebesgue’s criterion with a positive-measure nowhere-dense fat Cantor set. The item uses its indicator to refute the proposed nowhere-dense characterization.

The source establishes that Thomae’s nonnegative function is Riemann integrable with integral zero although it is not identically zero. The item packages this as a counterexample to the false pointwise conclusion.

The source gives finite rational-point indicators converging pointwise to the non-Riemann-integrable Dirichlet function. The item adapts the construction to a fixed enumeration and verifies each approximant’s integrability.
The source computes the lower and upper sums for x squared on uniform partitions and obtains integral one third. The item expands the finite-sum algebra in the library’s notation.
The sources give refinement monotonicity and standard Darboux-sum computations. The exact x-squared partitions and numerical comparison are a local worked example.
The university exercise treats the floor function’s Riemann integrability and integral by integer subintervals. The item specializes to its chosen interval and spells out the Darboux sums.
The lecture notes state that the Cantor-set indicator is Riemann integrable with integral zero. The item verifies its discontinuity set and applies Lebesgue’s criterion.
The sources establish Thomae’s integrability and zero integral. The item gives both a discontinuity-set proof and direct Darboux control.
The sources show that every interval contains rationals and irrationals, forcing lower sums zero and upper sums one for the Dirichlet indicator. The item reproduces that standard proof.
The lecture notes state that the fat-Cantor-set indicator is not Riemann integrable. The item identifies the positive-measure discontinuity set and applies Lebesgue’s criterion.

The sources give the F-sigma characterization of discontinuity sets and Lebesgue’s criterion. The item supplies a particular weighted closed-set-indicator construction for a prescribed null F-sigma set.

The sources show the Dirichlet function is not Riemann integrable and explain the universal fine-partition quantifier. The item constructs one rational-tagged uniform sequence whose sums nevertheless converge.
The source gives Thomae’s nonnegative, nonzero, Riemann-integrable function with integral zero. The item records it as the direct counterexample and checks a positive value.
